newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbian opposition stages fifth day of protests.
newsitem.headline: Serbian opposition stages fifth day of protests.

text.p: Serbian opposition parties launched fresh protests on Friday to demand President Slobodan Milosevic's ruling Socialists accept defeat in municipal elections.
Some 1,000 university students marched through the centre of Belgrade to back the opposition coalition which accuses the Socialists of trying to annul their victory in local polls.
Rain appeared to dampen tempers in the capital. Around 10,000 people, including the students, gathered in a crowd about half the size of yesterday's biggest demonstration in years.
Independent trade union Nezavisnost appealed to Serbs to leave their factories, offices, classrooms and fields and prevent the fraud "otherwise the authorities will roll over us."
Opposition leaders say the authorities have committed massive fraud by annulling votes which gave the opposition victories in 15 of the 18 biggest towns in Serbia at local elections last Sunday.
Opposition leader Zoran Djindjic said Milosevic's rule was under unprecedented threat after five days of protests across the republic.
"It (the election victory) puts in question the basic principles of his authority," Djindjic told Reuters.
"Milosevic is not losing much in terms of real power but psychologically he's losing a lot. There is going to be a chain reaction," he said.
Djindjic heads the Democratic Party (DS), one of three parties allied in the opposition Zajedno (Together) coalition, and is expected to become the next mayor of Belgrade.
Analysts say the opposition victory has taken the Socialists by total surprise prompting them to resort to annullments.
This has provoked an outcry both at home and abroad and alienated some members of the leftist coalition which scored a resounding victory at federal elections almost three weeks ago.

Nova Democratija, close to Milosevic, on Thursday denounced election rigging and called for the will of the people to be respected. Its headquarters were bombed hours later, independent Belgrade Radio B92 reported.
Expectations that electoral commissions and courts might deliver rulings on ballot results on Friday went unmet with the judicial bodies apparently biding their time.
"Unofficially we have heard that the Socialists have managed to contest another 13 seats in the Belgrade assembly," Dragor Hribar, another Democratic Party leader told B92 radio.
The Socialists, putting up a major fight elsewhere in Serbia, had previously conceded defeat in Belgrade saying Zajedno had won 60 out of the 110 seats in the city assembly.

In the industrial town of Nis, where the opposition said it won by a wide margin, a local electoral commission gave the Socialists victory by awarding them extra seats due to unspecified irregularities.
Some 10,000 people were protesting there on Friday.

Milosevic has already been warned by the United States to improve his poor political and human rights record if he wants to see the lifting of an "outer wall" of sanctions which blocks desperately-needed foreign capital from Belgrade.
The United States and Britain have voiced grave concerns over the opposition's allegations and France on Friday called for restraint from all sides.
